n: An unnamed “man of God” from Judah arrives at Bethel at the very moment Jeroboam is standing at his new altar to offer incense. He comes by the Lord’s command.

f.g: a common title for a prophet.

n: He prophesies that a future king of David’s line, Josiah, will burn the bones of these false priests on this very altar. Remarkably, he names Josiah about three hundred years before Josiah fulfilled it.

f.w: men's bones shall be burnt upon thee
f.g: burning bones on an altar would defile it permanently.

n: To confirm the prophecy, he gives an immediate sign: the altar will split and its ashes spill out.
Jeroboam points and orders the prophet seized—but his outstretched arm withers and freezes in place. The king’s power is no match for God’s word.
The sign is fulfilled at once: the altar cracks and its ashes pour out.
Jeroboam begs the prophet to pray for him. The man of God does, and the king’s hand is healed—a display of mercy even toward an opponent.

f.w: Entreat now the face of the LORD

n: The king now tries hospitality and a reward—perhaps to win the prophet over or make it look as though he endorsed Bethel.
The prophet refuses even if offered half the palace. Eating together would signal fellowship with a corrupt worship.
His instructions were strict: eat nothing, drink nothing, and go home a different way. The commands symbolized total separation from Bethel’s apostasy.
He obeys and leaves by another road.
An old prophet living in Bethel hears from his sons everything that happened.
He asks which way the man of God went.
He has his donkey saddled and sets out.
He finds the man of God resting under an oak—having lingered, perhaps, when he should have hurried home.

f.g: or terebinth, a large shade tree.

n: The old prophet invites him home for a meal.
The man of God refuses at first, repeating the Lord’s command.
He clearly remembers exactly what the Lord said.
The old prophet lies, claiming an angel told him to bring the man back. The lesson: a claimed revelation from another person does not override what God has plainly told you directly.

f.g: his motive is not given—perhaps to test him or to win honor for Bethel.

n: The man of God goes back and eats and drinks, breaking the Lord’s command.
In a startling twist, the true word of the Lord now comes through the lying prophet.
He declares that the man of God has disobeyed the Lord’s direct command.
His punishment: he will not be buried in his family tomb—a grave dishonor in Israelite culture, meaning he will die away from home.
After the meal, the old prophet saddles a donkey for him.
On the road a lion kills him. Strangely, the lion does not eat him or the donkey; both simply stand by the body. The scene shows this was a deliberate act of God, not a random attack.
Passersby see the eerie sight and report it in Bethel.
The old prophet recognizes that the word of the Lord has been fulfilled.
He sets out again.
He finds the body untouched, with the lion and donkey still standing by—confirming God’s hand.
He brings the body back to Bethel to mourn and bury him.
He buries him in his own tomb and laments, “Alas, my brother!”—a traditional cry of grief.
He asks to be buried beside the man of God, perhaps hoping his bones would be spared when Josiah came.

f.w: lay my bones beside his bones

n: He affirms that the prophecy against Bethel’s altar will certainly be fulfilled. “Samaria” here refers to the northern region, named after the city built later.

f.g: the northern kingdom’s towns; Samaria city was built later (1 Kings 16:24).

n: Despite seeing a withered hand, a split altar, and a dramatic prophecy, Jeroboam does not repent. He keeps ordaining anyone who wants to be a priest.

f.g: literally ‘filled his hand’—installed him as priest.

n: This sin eventually destroys Jeroboam’s whole dynasty—fulfilled when Baasha wipes out his family.
